reconcile.connective: Tyndale's editors name all four positions directly, reading Mark's absolute wording as the core principle rather than excluding Matthew's and Paul's exceptions.

discrepancy.connective: The Skeptic's Annotated Bible catalogs these four positions as flatly incompatible statements about whether divorce is ever allowed.

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, Skeptic's Annotated Bible (1999), contra/divorce.html

excerpts.excerpt_text: The parallel in Luke 16:18 agrees with Mark and mentions no exceptions to this prohibition of divorce, while Matthew’s parallel account allows an exception in cases of infidelity (Matt 19:9; see also Matt 5:32). Paul also allows an exception if an unbelieving partner deserts the marriage (1 Cor 7:15). Mark’s account focuses on the core principles—God hates divorce (Mal 2:16), marriage is meant to be for life, and divorce betrays the divine purpose of marriage.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: This is the one note in the gathered set that names all four canon positions (Mark's/Luke's absolute wording, Matthew's porneia exception, Paul's desertion exception) together and states the harmonizing frame that Mark gives the core principle rather than an exhaustive rule excluding the others.

pd_work.resource: John Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874)
pd_work.author: John Haley
pd_work.note: Haley's 'Ethical Discrepancies' chapter pairs Deut 24:1-2 against Matt 5:32, Matt 19:7-8, and Luke 16:18 under the heading 'Divorce — Largely allowed. / Restricted,' arguing Moses' concession, granted 'because of the hardness of your hearts,' was tightened rather than contradicted by Christ's stricter standard (curl+grep-confirmed at examinationofall00hale_djvu.txt, ETHICAL DISCREPANCIES chapter, p. 263).

link.title: GotQuestions: What does the Bible say about divorce and remarriage?
link.note: Live apologetic treatment covering Matthew's porneia exception, Paul's 1 Corinthians 7:15 desertion exception, and Deuteronomy 24 as a hardness-of-heart concession; it does not directly address why Mark and Luke omit any exception clause.
